svg.aria-label: Lime kiln and slaking quicklime: a simple shaft kiln (earth kiln) is dug into a hillside, loaded from the top of the slope and emptied at the bottom; the kiln chamber is cylindrical or egg-shaped, about 1.5-2.5 m inside diameter and about 2-4 m high; the earth bank is the insulation; the inside is lined with fire-resistant stones or bricks, with the joints sealed with clay; at one side of the base is the fire door / draw hole for adding fuel and air and for raking out the lime when the firing is done; stones laid across the bottom form a grate so air comes in from below; the top opening is for loading and letting smoke out. Mixed firing: lay kindling at the bottom, then load alternate layers of fuel (coal, coke, charcoal) and limestone upwards. Separate firing: build an arch of large limestone blocks laid dry at the bottom of the kiln, with the firebox under the arch; keep feeding wood at the fire door and the flames pass up through the stone. Firing: a low, slow fire on the first day; increase the fire gradually and keep the inside of the kiln bright red to orange-yellow, about 900-1000°C; dull red means the temperature is too low; a wood-fired kiln is kept at full fire for 2-4 days without letting the fire die; when done, close the fire door and cool slowly for 1-2 days before emptying; do not throw water into a hot kiln; rake the lime out through the draw hole with a long-handled rake; do not go into the kiln or stand on its top; there is carbon monoxide on top of the kiln and downwind. Slaking: quicklime plus water becomes slaked lime and gives off a lot of heat; put the water in first, then add lumps of quicklime in batches, using about 3-4 times as much water as quicklime by weight; stir with a long-handled wooden rake, standing well back with your face turned away; do not pour a little water onto a big heap of lime, as it boils locally and spatters; do not use plastic buckets or tubs, as the temperature can approach 100°C; strain out the grit into the storage pit and keep a layer of water over the putty; maturing: at least 2 weeks for masonry, at least 1 month for plastering and limewash. Safety: wear goggles, gloves and long sleeves and keep a bucket of clean water beside you; if it gets in the eyes, wipe away particles around the eye, then at once hold the eyelids open and rinse continuously with plenty of clean water, and see a doctor as soon as possible; on the skin, first brush off the dry powder, then rinse with plenty of clean water

3. When done, close the fire door and cool

Strain out unslaked grit → into the storage pit, keep a layer of water on top → mature
Maturing: at least 2 weeks for masonry, at least 1 month for plastering and limewash
(lets overburnt particles finish slaking in the pit, so they do not "pop" in the wall)
⚠️ Quicklime gets violently hot with water and can boil it;
dust or slurry in the eyes can cause blindness
✓ When handling quicklime, slaking it or mixing mortar, wear goggles, gloves and
long sleeves, and keep a bucket of clean water beside you
In the eyes: wipe away particles around the eye, then at once hold the eyelids
open and rinse continuously with plenty of clean water; see a doctor as soon as possible
On the skin: first brush (wipe) off the dry powder, then rinse with plenty of clean
water; do not splash a little water on first
